Most climbing training programs assume the climber can always get to the same wall or training space super regularly. 

But how does a climber maintain strength and keep conditioning alive when their location and time keep changing?

Because life isn’t always simple, our portable equipment has created a different outcome for tens-of-thousands of climbers since 2008. 

So you are psyched for climbing, but perhaps you are a shift worker, travel for work, rent an apartment or home where you cannot install equipment, are on an extended climbing trip, have family responsibilities or want to train in private and the list goes on …

How does a 9a redpointer, World Champ Ice Climber and pro climber train? 👀

Here’s a little peak at one of our athletes @angelika_rainer in her current autumn & winter training block…

Board climbing - an absolute staple of almost every high level climber we work with. Movement patterns to fit climbing projects, hand-to-toe tension weaknesses to be addressed & AnCap work for conversion into route climbing later on…

S&C - an emphasis on upper body raw pulling strength and posterior chain tension and strength. Most climbers will develop some of this on the wall, but top end strength will generally be developed off-wall. 

Aerobic endurance - 4x4s on a less steep system board are incredibly convenient and hit that midway slot between “aero” and “anaerobic” endurance. Depending on the length of route project, this will be moderated up or down in total training focus. 

Angelika’s goals for this coming year are twofold. In the short term this autumn she has a couple of 8c’s she’s checking out and then going into the full winter period it’s prep for another 9a! We’re psyched to be supporting another athlete out there living their climbing dreams 🙌💪

I don’t always have time for a proper workout.
So I stopped waiting for one.

Three days a week, I pick a window of up to three hours while I’m working.

Depending on the workflow, every few minutes I stop for one short, high-intensity set — then I get straight back to work.

It might be weighted pull-ups.
Push-ups.
L-sits.
Or whatever fits that day.

No dedicated hour. No complete workout session.

Just a few hard sets spread throughout the day.

For me, it’s a simple way to keep training even when work takes up most of my time.

A few minutes are easier to find than an hour.

The Sunset Wall on the North side of the Cirque of the Moon has remained unclimbed since the first routes in this zone were put up in the late 70’s. Over the past 2 years, I have attempted the East face via 3 different routes across 4 separate attempts.

This year, we returned to the Cirque of the Moon for the past 2 weeks with the main goal of finishing this route and exploring other faces. On Sunday Aug 16th Brad and I summited the Sunset Wall — after fixing initial pitches and spending one night on the wall. Initially we had planned to pull ropes and complete it in one continuous push but after cleaning and straightening the line out we ran out of time. 

In addition to this, @photoswithdell and I established a new route on the previously unclimbed Sunset Buttress (“Buffalo Crude” was thought to be on this face, but is actually on Sumac Point) which surmounts in a sick 30m tight hands to hands dihedral! Adele and @lampshade4hat established a new 6p ~5.9 line up the right side of Sumac Point (not pictured), and Adele and I established a new 4p ~5.8 route on the right side of lower Sumac Point, chasing a major dihedral system (not pictured). All information can be found on Mountain Project!

Psyched to have the support of @metoliusclimbing to accomplish these goals and big thanks to @allensdiamond4ranch for getting all our stuff as close as possible!

Rebecca Vincent @beccacvincent sending her project at World Wall (North Bend, WA) on Sunday -- Pornstar, 5.13d, and a 2nd female ascent. Audrey Sniezek @audreysniezek sent it in 2011. Photo: Ryan Daudistel @rdaudistel

FAILURE HAS LEVELS.

20 mm edge. Added weight. And pull.

Once I hit my limit, I drop some weight and keep going.

Limit again. Drop the rest.

Then it’s just bodyweight, tired fingers and whatever pulling strength is left.

Basically a drop set — but on a 20 mm edge.

For climbing, strength isn’t only about how hard you can pull when you’re fresh. It’s also about how much you can still produce when your fingers and pulling muscles are already tired.

Training close to failure can be a useful tool for that. But going all the way to failure every time isn’t necessary — and probably isn’t a great idea either.

This is not how I train every session.

Sometimes I just like to see how many levels “I’m done” actually has.

Turns out: more than one.#climbingtraining #pullup

Version v.4.5.0 of the Lattice app is here! 🚀 What's new? 👇⁣
⁣
🧠 1. A Smarter, Goal-Driven Plan⁣
We've added a question to the plan generation quiz with smart branching questions. Choose your plan objective:⁣
➡️ Build Strength & Fitness (Long-term gains)⁣
➡️ Feel Good Climbing (Stay fresh and perform right now)⁣
➡️ Peak for an Event/Project (Targeting a specific goal within a timeframe)⁣
⁣
🔎 2. Training Focus⁣
You can now choose a specific training focus⁣
➡️ Forearm fitness⁣
➡️ Finger strength⁣
➡️ Balanced (combo of the two)⁣
(We're only just getting started with focus… more are coming!)⁣
⁣
📈 3. Ramp Weeks⁣
When your plan ends, you'll now have the option to skip the initial ramp week and dive straight into your new training. All first plans do still include a ramp week to help you ease in and reduce the risk of injury.⁣
⁣
⏱️ 4. Edit Sets in Timer ⁣
You asked, we delivered! You can now add or delete sets directly from the timer screen mid-workout. Anything you change carries straight through to your workout log. (Up next: editing reps and total time!)⁣
⁣
💬 5. Chat Improvements (For Climbing Training Plan PLUS users)⁣
Day-to-day communication just got smoother. We’ve fixed the unread message bug, added a 'New messages' divider, and made sure the screen stays awake while you're recording voice messages to your coach.⁣
⁣
Plus, we've resolved a bunch of other small bugs. Thanks to everyone has reported an issue or made a suggestion!⁣
⁣

Start a LatticePlan NOW - starts with a 7-day FREE trial!⁣

What happened next was something I never expected.

Since then, the orders just haven’t stopped coming in. No matter how much I produce, it always feels like I’m falling behind. While I’m working through one batch, new orders and inquiries keep piling up.

Climb with intention, improve faster ⚡️
Bouldering with no plan is fun, but adding a little structure with Intentional Sessions can help you learn more every time you step on the wall. 
Want to build strength or train specifics for a project? 
➡️ Max Effort Session 💥
Climb problems that are at your limit where linking moves is a win. Expect a high failure rate and low chance of a full send, making sure you rest between attempts. Do this when you’re feeling fresh and strong, and stop the session when quality starts to drop (ie. you’re no longer working max strength)
Want to build session fitness, or expand your movement skillset?
➡️ Mileage Session 🏃
Climb A LOT of problems with a high success rate. Choose problems that are challenging but can be done within a few attempts. Make sure to climb a variety of styles and wall angles. 
Want to improve on a specific technique, or target a certain weakness? 
➡️ Skill Session 🎯
Find climbs that use your chosen skill– heel hooks, body tension, slopers, etc. Try to incorporate the skill where you can, even if it feels silly! Vary the intensity and climb on a range of terrain. You can use this as a warm-up or the focus of a whole session.
💡 Mix it up each session! Focus on capacity early on in your training cycle, then more intensity closer to your peak.
Take your training into your own hands! Learn all about exercise selection and intentional climbing sessions in ‘A Climber’s Guide to Training’ 👇

Power on steep terrain: Drag vs. Crimp 💥
If you want more power on steep terrain, it’s not just about finger strength — it’s how you use your grip.
When using a closed grip (half crimp/full crimp), your elbow can travel higher (increased angle) without losing contact. That means:
✅ More force
✅ Longer time to apply force
✅ Mechanically better grip when catching the next hold
An open drag is great for conserving energy, but it limits upward drive and reduces force production time for the same reason - your elbow just can't go that high around the hold.
If you're going big on steep terrain, switch to a closed grip and turn that pull into a powerful push.
